header: Date: 2025-02-26 | Time: 17:00 UTC | Duration: 52m | Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Martinez (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Atlas), Tom Reynolds (Atlas), Sanjay Patel (Atlas)
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on app integration: SDK usage, function/tool calling reliability, and structured output. Reviewed latest pilot results (latency and error rates), discussed retry behavior and schema enforcement for structured JSON responses, and agreed on next steps: Dedicated config proposal, SDK samples, smoke tests, and a load test scheduling.
transcript:
[00:00] Avery Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, then we will jump into the SDK integration items and the structured output failures Priya mentioned.
[00:12] Priya Nair: Yep, this is Priya, Tom and Sanjay are here as well. Thanks.
[00:18] Diego Martinez: Morning all, Diego from Redwood SE. I grabbed the logs you uploaded, Priya - thanks, those were super helpful.
[00:25] Tom Reynolds: quick note, we had two main asks this week: reduce hallucinated fields in the structured output and make function calls more deterministic.
[00:37] Priya Nair: yeah the function-calling path sometimes returns a 200 but the body is malformed, like missing the id field or returning arrays where we expect objects. Could be our prompt or the SDK layer.
[00:49] Diego Martinez: right, we saw a couple patterns. One is streaming partial JSON which the current parser in your app treats as final. The SDK has a helper to accumulate stream chunks and validate JSON - did you use that?
[01:04] Priya Nair: we wired the quickstart example but not the stream-accumulator helper, we assumed the SDK would hand us finished JSON.
[01:12] Avery Chen: okay that's something Diego can send as a snippet. Also for the function/tool calling, we noticed retry behavior - if a tool fails at the infra layer (like 502 from your internal tool) the SDK will retry twice by default, which can lead to duplicate side-effects if your tool isn't idempotent.
[01:29] Sanjay Patel: that's important for us - our downstream order service isn't idempotent for certain POST endpoints. Any recommended pattern?
[01:36] Diego Martinez: two options: add an idempotency key at the tool layer (we can surface that in the SDK example) or change retry policy to no-retry and handle retries at the app level after verification. We can provide sample middleware.
[01:50] Tom Reynolds: about latency - Priya you shared the 95th numbers? I think you said 350ms for the small prompt and 1.8s for the end-to-end including tool calls?
[01:59] Priya Nair: yes, roughly. The raw generation median is 120ms on Redwood hosted model, but with a tool call that does a DB lookup and then we serialize back it's 1.6-1.9s.
[02:10] Avery Chen: that aligns with our expectations. For POC cost/latency tradeoffs: if you move heavy pre- or post-processing into your infra the token cost drops but latency may increase - depending on where you want to spend time.
[02:23] Priya Nair: one more item - structured output validation. We tried strict JSON schema validation and it failed on about 8% of responses, mostly small deviations (nulls, extra commas, wrong field names).
[02:36] Diego Martinez: couple tactics: 1) schema-first prompting with examples (few-shot), 2) use the SDK's structured-output helper that does a two-pass: first generate then call a small verification function (like micro-eval) to repair minor issues, 3) accept a looser schema at the edge and enforce in a post-processing step.
[02:52] Tom Reynolds: can you show an example of the two-pass repair?
[02:56] Diego Martinez: sure - I'll paste a snippet after the call; the gist is you run the model to produce a JSON blob and then invoke a small function that attempts to coerce types and fill defaults, and if it still fails, fall back to a deterministic template. It reduces failures from 8% to under 1% in our tests.
[03:12] Priya Nair: that sounds great; the question is whether that two-pass adds too much latency.
[03:17] Diego Martinez: it's typically an extra 80-150ms on average if you run it as a quick verification. If that's unacceptable, the other path is to tighten the prompt and increase sampling determinism which helps but can slightly increase cost.
[03:30] Avery Chen: quick note on Dedicated vs Hosted: since you mentioned data residency and SSO, Dedicated gives better isolation and predictable throughput for your load, but it requires a short onboarding window. We'll send config recommendations.
[03:44] Sanjay Patel: also we need VPC peering and KMS integration for keys - can you confirm Redwood supports customer-managed KMS?
[03:52] Avery Chen: yes, customer-managed KMS is supported on Private/Dedicated plans; on hosted we do envelope encryption with BYOK options in the roadmap. We'll attach the security brief.
[04:03] Tom Reynolds: regarding SDK integration, Priya and our mobile lead noticed an edge case where streaming responses cause partial function calls; the mobile app invoked the function as soon as it saw the function name token.
[04:16] Diego Martinez: right, that's the streaming partial results issue I mentioned. The SDK has a second API - "on_complete" emitter - that fires when a function call is fully parsed. We'll include a mobile example to avoid premature invocation.
[04:31] Priya Nair: sample test results - we ran 1,000 requests with a mixed workload: 60% simple chat, 40% function-calling. Error rate for function-calls was 6.2% when using naive parsing, down to 0.9% when using the SDK helper. Latency p95 for function-calls was 1.85s naive vs 1.95s with helper (extra buffering).
[04:52] Avery Chen: those numbers are useful. Our recommendation is to use the helper and accept the 100ms delta for dramatically better correctness. Also consider batch mode for peaks to drop unit token cost.
[05:05] Tom Reynolds: can we get an estimate of cost delta if we use the helper vs not?
[05:10] Avery Chen: the helper itself doesn't change tokens, but it might increase request duration causing slightly higher compute time if you're on Dedicated with fixed GPU schedule; we'll include cost scenarios in the pricing doc.
[05:22] Priya Nair: question on tool auth - our internal tool requires a signed JWT per call. Will the SDK pass through headers or do we need a proxy?
[05:31] Diego Martinez: SDK can forward custom headers to the tool endpoint; for security we recommend a signed short-lived token generated by your infra. We'll add an example of signing middleware.
[05:40] Tom Reynolds: any known issues with KV cache and function calling if we rely on prefix caching?
[05:45] Diego Martinez: prefix/KV cache is mostly for tokens; tool calls are external and not cached by default. If you have deterministic tool results, you can cache them at the app layer but be careful with sensitive data.
[05:58] Priya Nair: on structured output schema - we saw fields sometimes camelCase vs snake_case, can we coerce naming with the verification function?
[06:06] Diego Martinez: yes, the repair step can normalize keys, coerce types, fill defaults. We'll provide a toy sanitizer.
[06:14] Avery Chen: okay let's run through the agreed next steps and owners. Diego will share the SDK snippet for stream accumulation and the two-pass verifier; Avery will share Dedicated config and pricing; Priya/Sanjay will run the smoke tests and upload logs; we'll schedule the load test for the week of 2025-03-10.
[06:31] Tom Reynolds: sounds good. One last thing - can Redwood run a short benchmark with our sample prompt to get a realistic p95 under Dedicated?
[06:38] Avery Chen: yes we can run a bench, we just need your sample prompts and expected volume; we'll coordinate offline.
[06:45] Priya Nair: I'll put the prompt set and expected traffic in the shared folder later today.
[06:51] Diego Martinez: perfect, I'll start prepping the SDK examples and post them in the same folder.
[06:55] Sanjay Patel: thanks everyone.
[06:57] Avery Chen: thanks, we'll follow up with docs and pricing. Bye.
[06:59] [meeting end]
